_export_meta.adaptation_notes: BTEC Tech Award Component 3 covers 'lifestyle factors' and 'life events' as two distinct lessons — closer alignment than L5. Reuse the lifestyle/life-event framing pattern but adapt content: this spec specifies named lifestyle subcategories (aerobic / muscle-strengthening / bone-strengthening activity; binge drinking vs abuse vs dependence) and lists named life events that must be reproduced. Critically, this spec adds the interrelation step (1.2.3 final paragraph) requiring students to chain life factor + lifestyle + life event to a PIES impact — that synthesis layer must be added fresh.

source_lesson.title: Lifestyle Factors Affecting Health
source_lesson.description: How nutrition, exercise, smoking, and substance misuse affect health and wellbeing.
source_lesson.content_html:
Why Lifestyle Factors Matter

Unlike inherited conditions, lifestyle factors are things people can control. The choices a person makes about what they eat, how active they are, and whether they smoke or misuse substances directly affect their health and wellbeing. The Component 3 specification identifies four key lifestyle factors: nutrition, physical activity, smoking, and substance misuse.

Each lifestyle factor can have both positive and negative effects on health and wellbeing. A balanced diet supports good physical health, while a poor diet increases the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The exam will often ask you to explain how a specific lifestyle factor affects an individual across the PIES categories.

Nutrition

Nutrition refers to the food and drink a person consumes and how the body uses it. A balanced diet provides the right amounts of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water. Good nutrition supports physical growth, brain function, emotional stability, and the energy needed to socialise and participate in activities.

Key Fact

A balanced diet positively affects all areas of PIES: physical (healthy weight, energy, strong immune system), intellectual (brain function, concentration), emotional (stable mood, positive self-image), social (energy to socialise, shared meals with others).

Poor nutrition includes both malnutrition (not getting enough nutrients) and over-nutrition (eating too much of the wrong foods). Malnutrition can weaken the immune system, slow growth in young people, and cause tiredness. Over-nutrition leads to obesity, which increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, CVD, and joint problems. Both affect emotional wellbeing through low energy and poor self-image, and social wellbeing through reduced ability to participate in activities.

Physical Activity

Regular physical activity is essential for maintaining good health. The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend that adults do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, while children and young people should aim for 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day.

The benefits of regular physical activity span all areas of PIES. Physically, it strengthens the heart, muscles, and bones, helps maintain a healthy weight, and reduces the risk of CVD, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers. Intellectually, exercise improves concentration, memory, and cognitive function by increasing blood flow to the brain. Emotionally, physical activity releases endorphins (natural mood-boosting chemicals), reduces stress and anxiety, and improves self-esteem. Socially, team sports and group exercise classes provide opportunities to meet people and build friendships.

A lack of physical activity (a sedentary lifestyle) has the opposite effect. It increases the risk of obesity, weakens muscles and bones, reduces concentration, worsens mood, and limits social opportunities. Prolonged inactivity is linked to higher rates of depression and anxiety.

Smoking

Smoking tobacco is one of the biggest preventable causes of ill health in the UK. Cigarettes contain nicotine (which is highly addictive), tar (which damages the lungs), and carbon monoxide (which reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry).

Physical: Smoking causes lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), heart disease, and strokes. It reduces lung capacity, causes breathlessness, and ages the skin prematurely. Intellectual: Reduced oxygen supply to the brain can impair concentration and memory. Emotional: While smokers often say smoking reduces stress, the addiction cycle actually increases anxiety between cigarettes. Worrying about health consequences adds further stress. Social: Smoking can cause social exclusion as non-smokers may avoid being around smoke. The cost of cigarettes reduces money available for social activities. Smoking bans in public places limit where smokers can go.

Key Fact

Smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in the UK. It damages the lungs, heart, and blood vessels, and the nicotine in tobacco creates a powerful addiction that makes quitting extremely difficult.

Substance Misuse

Substance misuse means using substances in a way that is harmful to health. The specification names three substances: alcohol, cannabis, and opiates (e.g. heroin).

Alcohol: Excessive drinking damages the liver (leading to cirrhosis), increases the risk of heart disease and some cancers, impairs judgement and coordination, and can lead to addiction (alcoholism). It affects emotional wellbeing through mood swings and depression, and social wellbeing through damaged relationships, aggression, and financial problems. The UK CMO guidelines recommend no more than 14 units per week for both men and women.

Cannabis: This is an illegal drug that can be smoked or eaten. It affects concentration, memory, and motivation. Long-term use is linked to mental health problems including anxiety, paranoia, and psychosis. It can also damage the lungs when smoked. Socially, cannabis use can lead to legal problems, reduced employment prospects, and damaged relationships.

Opiates (e.g. heroin): Opiates are highly addictive drugs that depress the central nervous system. Heroin use carries risks of overdose (which can be fatal), infections from sharing needles (including HIV and hepatitis), collapsed veins, and severe constipation. Addiction dominates the user’s life, leading to loss of employment, breakdown of relationships, criminal behaviour to fund the habit, and homelessness. Opiates have devastating effects across all areas of PIES.

Substance misuse does not just affect the individual — it impacts families, friendships, and communities. Children growing up with a parent who misuses substances may experience neglect, emotional trauma, and instability. The financial cost of addiction can push families into poverty.
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about lifestyle factors, always use the PIES framework to structure your answer. State the factor, explain the effect on a specific PIES area, then develop the point by showing the consequence. For case study questions, link every point back to the named individual — generic answers that do not reference the case study will not reach the highest mark bands.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lifestyle factors (nutrition, physical activity, smoking, substance misuse) are choices that can positively or negatively affect health and wellbeing across all PIES areas.
  • Good nutrition and regular physical activity support physical health, brain function, emotional stability, and social participation.
  • Smoking and substance misuse (alcohol, cannabis, opiates) create addiction, damage physical health, and have devastating effects on emotional and social wellbeing.

practice_questions.text: Identify one lifestyle factor that can affect an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for one correct identification:
• Nutrition (1)
• Physical activity (1)
• Smoking (1)
• Substance misuse (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two ways that regular physical activity can benefit an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct benefit (max 2):
• Strengthens the heart/muscles/bones (1)
• Helps maintain a healthy weight (1)
• Reduces risk of CVD/type 2 diabetes (1)
• Releases endorphins/improves mood (1)
• Improves concentration/memory (1)
• Provides social opportunities (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how smoking can have a negative effect on an individual's physical and social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for developed explanation:
• Physically, smoking causes lung damage/COPD/cancer (1) because tar builds up in the lungs and carbon monoxide reduces oxygen in the blood (1).
• Socially, smoking can cause exclusion (1) because non-smokers may avoid being around smoke and smoking bans in public places limit where smokers can socialise (1).
• Accept other valid developed points.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of poor nutrition on an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion covering multiple PIES areas with developed points.
Mid band (3-4): Some discussion with partial development.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points with little development.
Indicative content:
• Physical: over-nutrition leads to obesity, increasing risk of CVD and type 2 diabetes; malnutrition weakens immune system and slows growth
• Intellectual: lack of nutrients affects brain function, concentration at school/work
• Emotional: poor diet linked to low energy and poor self-image; obesity may cause low self-esteem
• Social: reduced energy to socialise; obesity may lead to bullying and withdrawal
• Links: poor nutrition leads to physical health problems which then affect emotional and social wellbeing.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which substance misuse has a greater impact on health and wellbeing than smoking.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
Substance misuse:
• Opiates carry risk of fatal overdose — immediate life-threatening danger
• Heroin addiction dominates life — loss of job, home, relationships
• Sharing needles risks HIV and hepatitis
• Alcohol causes liver cirrhosis, brain damage, and aggression
• Cannabis linked to psychosis and mental health problems
Smoking:
• Leading preventable cause of death in the UK
• Long-term risks: lung cancer, COPD, heart disease, stroke
• Highly addictive due to nicotine
• Effects are cumulative — may take years to develop
• Social exclusion and financial cost
Conclusion: Substance misuse (especially opiates) may have more immediate and severe effects, but smoking kills more people overall because it is more widespread. Both have devastating impacts and the significance depends on the substance, frequency of use, and individual circumstances.

practice_questions.text: Priya is 17 years old. She has started drinking alcohol at weekends with friends and has recently tried cannabis. She has been skipping meals and her school attendance has dropped. Her parents are worried about her behaviour. Using the case study, assess how Priya's lifestyle factors are affecting her overall health and wellbeing. Consider the impact on her physical, intellectual, emotional, and social development.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive response covering all PIES areas with clear links to Priya's specific circumstances and chains of reasoning.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good coverage of multiple PIES areas with some links to the case study.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but limited development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to the case study.
Indicative content:
• Physical: Alcohol damages the liver and brain (still developing at 17). Skipping meals leads to malnutrition — weakened immune system, lack of energy. Cannabis damages lungs.
• Intellectual: Cannabis impairs concentration and memory. Skipping meals reduces brain function. Dropped school attendance means missed learning — affects academic achievement.
• Emotional: Alcohol is a depressant — may worsen mood. Cannabis linked to anxiety and paranoia. Conflict with parents causes stress. May feel guilt or worry about her behaviour.
• Social: Drinking with friends may seem positive socially, but risky behaviour can damage friendships. Conflict with parents strains family relationships. Dropped attendance reduces school friendships.
• Links: At 17, Priya is in adolescence where peer pressure is strong and brain development is ongoing — substance misuse at this age can have long-lasting effects. The combination of multiple negative lifestyle factors compounds the impact.
• Synoptic links: Parents' concern shows impact on family relationships (Component 1). Support services could help (Component 2).

glossary_terms.definition: Choices and behaviours that individuals make in their daily lives that can positively or negatively affect their health and wellbeing.
The process of taking in food and using it for growth, energy, and repair of the body.
Any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure, including walking, cycling, sports, and exercise.
A highly addictive chemical found in tobacco that stimulates the brain and creates dependency.
The harmful use of substances such as alcohol, cannabis, or opiates for purposes not consistent with medical or legal guidelines.
